header:
Date/Time: 2026-04-02 14:00 UTC
Duration: ~78 minutes
Location: Zoom call
Attendees: Ava Chen, Marco Ruiz (Redwood); Sophie Patel, David Kim, Liam O'Connor, Maya Singh (Brightline)
summary: Technical deep dive comparing Redwood Hosted vs Dedicated (and private/VPC) for Brightline's latency-sensitive inference workloads. Covered runtime optimizations (KV cache, batching, quantization), noisy-neighbor/isolation concerns, throughput guarantees, and networking/VPC constraints for on-prem deployments. Action items include sharing benchmark templates, Brightline providing traffic traces, and scheduling a PoC for VPC networking and KMS integration.
topics: isolation vs noisy neighbor on shared hosted pools
throughput guarantees and SLA for Dedicated
transcript:
[00:00] Ava (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. We're going to run through dedicated vs hosted with a focus on runtime perf, kv cache, batching and the VPC/on-prem ask.
[00:22] Sophie (Brightline): Thanks Ava. We've got latency SLOs around 200ms P95 for our chat summarization pipeline, and cost is a secondary but important goal.
[00:35] Marco (Redwood SE): Great, can you describe your traffic profile a bit? QPS, seq lengths, and peak windows?
[00:47] Sophie: We're currently at ~35 qps average, peaks to 180 qps for 10-15 minutes at times. Sequence lengths vary
mostly 128-512 tokens; some long form 2k in analytics jobs.
[01:10] David (CTO): Also we need isolation for PHI-ish metadata; regulatory team will want audit logs, KMS, and SSO.
[01:25] Marco: Understood. High level: hosted gives fastest TTV but is a shared pool
Redwood has policies to route and we do prefix caching, but noisy neighbor risk exists if you need full isolation. Dedicated gives isolated GPU pools, predictable throughput and the SLA-backed latency targets.
[01:52] Liam (Security): Quick question: can dedicated support our existing HSM and KMS for encryption keys, or do we have to use Redwood's?
[02:05] Ava: Dedicated supports customer-managed KMS/HSM via our private deployment options
there are integration steps but it's supported. We'll share the KMS integration doc.
[02:18] Marco: On the runtime side, two main levers: KV cache to avoid recomputing prefix tokens, and batching to increase GPU efficiency. They interact: big batches are great for throughput but can increase P95 latency for single-shot requests.
[02:40] Maya (ML Eng): Can you walk through an example? If we cache prefixes for repeated templates, how much latency do we save?
[02:52] Marco: Example: with a hot KV cache hit we avoid the O(seq_prefix) attention computations. For a 512 prefix that could be 40-120ms savings depending on model and quantization. On hosted most customers see 40-70% token compute reduction for chat-style reuse.
[03:18] Sophie: The transcriber sometimes writes KV as KV cash in our notes, ha.
[03:25] Marco: Yeah you'll see mis-transcriptions. Back to batching: Redwood uses continuous batching
requests flow into a batcher and we form micro-batches using latency SLO-aware windows. So for latency-sensitive routes we can keep windows small (e.g., 5-10ms) and rely on cache to hold latency down while sacrificing some throughput.
[03:55] David: How does quantization impact quality? We need medical summarization accuracy.
[04:05] Marco: Tradeoff depends on model. int8 usually has negligible quality delta for many LLMs with proper calibration. 4-bit/FP4 can be more risky; we recommend running evals on your prompt set. Redwood Optimize can suggest quant profiles and run offline evals to detect regressions.
[04:30] Sophie: If we go dedicated, can we set hard throughput guarantees? We saw a spike last quarter where a shared pool slowed us.
[04:41] Ava: Dedicated offers committed capacity and autoscale policies with headroom. We can contract a minimum guaranteed throughput for e.g., 100k tokens/sec across the pool and include latency targets in the SLA. That reduces noisy neighbor impact because it's not shared traffic.
[05:05] Liam: For VPC/on-prem, what's the networking pattern? Do requests still go through Redwood control plane?
[05:15] Marco: For private deployments we have a control plane that can be customer-hosted or Redwood-managed. Data plane for inference can live within customer's VPC; control plane APIs are used for orchestration. There are variations: fully on-prem air-gapped or VPC-peered variants. Latency from your app to the GPUs will depend on your network topology; we recommend colocating inference near the app where possible.
[05:46] Sophie: Any regular reports on noisy neighbor diagnostics in hosted?
[05:52] Ava: We provide per-route latency breakdowns and token-level profiling in the Console. If you see regression we can triage with traces and if necessary migrate you to a Dedicated pool.
[06:08] David: Let's talk cold-starts and KV cache warmup. If we spin a new dedicated node, how long until cache warms?
[06:19] Marco: Warmup depends on prefix patterns. For per-user chat where prefixes are unique, cache hit rate will be low; for template-based prompts it's quick. We also support pre-warming strategies: load popular prefixes at deployment time or keep warm spare capacity. Cold-start can add 100-300ms depending on sequence length and model.
[06:45] Maya: How does continuous batching affect memory/kv cache usage? If we batch many different requests, do we evict KV entries?
[06:56] Marco: The runtime's KV cache is sharded per worker and uses LRU with configurable TTLs and size limits. High batch concurrency increases working set, so you might see higher memory pressure; Dedicated lets you tune cache size per node for high-hit workloads.
[07:16] Sophie: We are also considering aggressive quantization to reduce GPU footprint. Is there a fast way to validate quality?
[07:26] Marco: Redwood Optimize includes an evaluation harness
upload a labeled prompt set and it will run quality comparisons across quantization/size variants and surface regressions. We encourage A/B testing on a small live traffic shadow.
[07:43] David: About costs
Dedicated seems pricier but predictable. Any rules of thumb?
[07:50] Ava: Hosted is OPEX-style pay-as-you-go; Dedicated is committed with lower unit cost for high steady throughput. If your 95th-percentile monthly tokens justify reserved capacity, Dedicated often wins on $/token. We can run a cost model once we have your profile.
[08:09] Liam: SSO and RBAC
do Dedicated and Private support our existing identity provider?
[08:16] Marco: Yes, SAML/SSO and SCIM provisioning are supported for Dedicated and Private. Audit logs and per-token tracing are available for enterprise plans.
[08:30] Sophie: A noisy neighbor scenario: what if another tenant is saturating NVLink or PCIe on a shared host
how does Redwood detect and mitigate?
[08:40] Marco: We monitor per-instance metrics and have heuristics for noisy-neighbor detection; mitigation can be automatic throttling or moving workloads. That said, if you require absolute isolation, Dedicated is the right path.
[08:57] David: For the PoC we want to reproduce our peak + a sudden burst pattern; can Redwood simulate that?
[09:05] Marco: Yes, we'll use your real traces in the benchmarking harness and run both hosted-simulated loads and dedicated cluster runs. We'll include KV cache warmup scenarios and mixed prompt lengths.
[09:22] Sophie: Can you describe how latency SLOs are enforced in the runtime?
[09:28] Marco: The runtime is SLO-aware: request queues are prioritized, there's early-exit policy for function-calls, and we run small micro-batches for latency routes. If a route consistently exceeds SLOs, we can route to smaller models or fall back to a cheaper/fast variant.
[09:49] Maya: What's the impact of model parallelism on per-request latency? For big models we need tensor parallelism
does that add overhead?
[09:58] Marco: TP adds cross-host comms; for large models latencies can increase due to all-reduce operations. Dedicated clusters with NVLink and optimized kernels reduce that overhead. We can provide per-model perf profiles.
[10:15] Liam: For compliance, do you keep decrypted logs anywhere?
[10:21] Ava: No, we don't store plaintext request content outside your retention policy; logs are pseudonymized and encrypted. Private deployments can keep logs entirely on-prem. We'll share the security paper.
[10:35] Sophie: On the KV cache eviction policy, can we pin prefixes?
[10:40] Marco: You can pin keys in Dedicated via APIs to avoid eviction
handy for commonly used templates. In hosted we offer TTL tuning but not explicit pinning for multi-tenant pool.
[10:55] David: How does the autoscaler behave under sudden burst? Does it slow things or spin up instantly?
[11:03] Marco: Autoscaling has two parts: reactive (spin new nodes based on queue/backlog) and predictive (based on historical patterns). Reaction takes time
tens of seconds to a few minutes depending on infra
so we recommend warm pools or burst capacity for ultra-low-latency SLAs.
[11:27] Sophie: If we choose Dedicated, what are typical lead times?
[11:31] Ava: Provisioning a Dedicated pool is usually a few days if in hosted cloud; for on-prem or VPC private it's longer due to networking and security approvals
often 2-6 weeks.
[11:46] Marco: Quick note on batching strategy: we support dynamic batching with latency windows and also deterministic batching for throughput jobs. For real-time routes you can set latency budget of e.g., 100ms and the batcher will try to fill batches within that.
[12:06] Sophie: Can Redwood do model distillation or smaller ensembles for faster latency?
[12:13] Marco: We can provide guidance; platform doesn't do distillation for you but Redwood Optimize can recommend smaller models/quant profiles. Many customers get good latency by switching to a distilled model for real-time inference and larger for background jobs.
[12:35] David: Any risks with KV cache and user privacy? If we cache prefixes that contain PII, is that stored encrypted?
[12:45] Marco: KV entries are encrypted at rest and can be configured to use customer-managed keys. For sensitive data we recommend tokenization/PII stripping at the application layer before caching.
[12:59] Sophie: Let's walk through a sample benchmark plan 
 what metrics should we collect?
[13:05] Marco: Collect P50/P95/P99 latency, CPU/GPU utilization, memory/KV cache hit rate, tokens/sec, error rate, and cold-start delta. Also trace per-token compute time if possible.
[13:25] Sophie: Do you have an example benchmark template?
[13:28] Marco: Yes we'll share the benchmark spreadsheet and harness link.
[13:32] Liam: For private on-prem, is there ongoing management from Redwood? Or do we have to run everything?
[13:39] Ava: We offer a managed private option where Redwood operates the control plane and provides support; fully self-managed on-prem is also possible for air-gapped customers.
[13:51] Maya: About quantization: any guardrails to prevent silent failures where text degrades subtly?
[13:57] Marco: That's why we emphasize evals and shadow testing. Redwood Optimize will run quality checks and flag regressions. We also recommend a human review sample on initial rollout.
[14:12] Sophie: If we move to Dedicated, can we isolate particular model endpoints to particular GPU types?
[14:18] Marco: Yes, you can map models to GPU pools
A100s for heavy models, T4s for cheaper ops. Scheduler respects pool affinity.
[14:30] David: For our use-case, we likely need a hybrid: Dedicated for low-latency public traffic, and hosted or cheaper pools for batch analytics. Any pitfalls?
[14:41] Marco: Hybrid is common. Pitfall is divergence in model versions and quant profiles; we recommend CI/CD for model config and unified rollout policies to avoid drift.
[14:55] Sophie: Are there examples of other healthcare customers on Dedicated?
[15:00] Ava: Yes we have a few enterprise healthcare customers
cannot name them on a public call but we can set up references under NDA.
[15:10] David: About throttling
if we hit token budget in hosted during a burst, will Redwood reject or queue?
[15:18] Marco: We can configure hard quotas to reject or soft quotas that queue/fallback. For production critical apps we usually recommend Dedicated or reserved burst capacity.
[15:33] Sophie: Any metrics about cache hit rates you can share?
[15:36] Marco: Typical chat-style workloads see 60-90% KV hit rates for templated prompts; for per-user unique chats it's lower, around 10-25%.
[15:50] Liam: For logging and tracing, can we keep traces for longer than default retention?
[15:55] Ava: Yes, higher-tier plans allow longer retention; for Private deployments you can set retention yourself.
[16:05] Sophie: Let's confirm next steps: Marco shares benchmark template, Sophie shares traffic trace, schedule PoC.
[16:12] Ava: We'll also send SOC2 and KMS docs and propose dates for the network PoC.
[16:20] David: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[16:24] Ava: Thanks all, we'll follow up with the artifacts and plan.
[16:30] [meeting ends early]
